final_method_items.summary: Given a set of newly created SSA names (NEW_SSA_NAMES) and a set of existing SSA names (OLD_SSA_NAMES), update the SSA form so that: 1- The names in OLD_SSA_NAMES dominated by the definitions of NEW_SSA_NAMES are all re-written to be reached by the appropriate definition from NEW_SSA_NAMES. 2- If needed, new PHI nodes are added to the iterated dominance frontier of the blocks where each of NEW_SSA_NAMES are defined. Note that the function assumes that the new defining statement has already been inserted in the IL. For instance, given the following code: 1 L0: 2 x_1 = PHI (0, x_5) 3 if (x_1 < 10) 4 if (x_1 > 7) 5 y_2 = 0 6 else 7 y_3 = x_1 + x_7 8 endif 9 x_5 = x_1 + 1 10 goto L0; 11 endif Suppose that we insert new names x_10 and x_11 (lines 4 and 8). 1 L0: 2 x_1 = PHI (0, x_5) 3 if (x_1 < 10) 4 x_10 = ... 5 if (x_1 > 7) 6 y_2 = 0 7 else 8 x_11 = ... 9 y_3 = x_1 + x_7 10 endif

behavior_items: The source defines one volatile global `a` and several non-volatile globals `b, c, d, e, f, g`. Because these globals are zero-initialized, the program has well-defined startup values even though most are never explicitly assigned in `main`. This matters because the optimizer can reason about many branches as initially depending on known zero values, while `volatile int a;` prevents the read expression `a;` inside the loop from being deleted as dead code.

`main` starts with two local integers, `i = 2` and `j = 1`, then uses a label `k:` to form an outer control-flow region that can be re-entered with `goto k` when `b` is nonzero. This creates irreducible-looking source structure from the optimizer’s point of view because a later conditional jumps back to an earlier label rather than using a structured loop construct.

The first branch `if (!e) ; else { ... }` guards the main interesting region. When `e == 0`, the body is skipped entirely. When `e != 0`, control enters a block containing a local `short l = 1`, a dead-looking `if (0)` with an attached label `m:`, a `for` loop over global `f`, and a final assignment `g = 0`. Even though `if (0)` is always false, the label `m:` remains a valid jump target for `goto m;`, so the block containing `d = g;` is semantically reachable through the jump.

The labeled statement is subtle: `if (0) m: d = g;` means normal fallthrough never executes `d = g`, but a jump to label `m` lands directly on that statement. This creates an alternate entry edge into code placed textually inside the `else` block. Compilers must preserve this CFG edge even if the guarding condition is constant false, because labels are not removed when targeted by a goto.

After the label region, the code sets `f = 0` and enters `for (; f < 2; f++)`. This loop has a fixed small trip-count in the simple case, making it an attractive candidate for complete unrolling during GCC’s `cunroll` pass. The bug report confirms the crash occurs during `tree_unroll_loops_completely` in `tree-ssa-loop-ivcanon.cc`, so the reproducer is specifically exercising loop-complete-unroll logic on a structurally awkward loop.

Inside the outer `for` loop, the statement `if (f) for (; j < 2; j++) if (i) goto m;` creates a nested loop that only becomes active on the second outer iteration (`f != 0`). Since `j` starts at 1, the inner loop condition `j < 2` initially allows one iteration. If `i` is nonzero, the loop performs `goto m;`, which jumps out of the nested loops to the earlier label, executing `d = g;` and then resuming at `f = 0` before re-entering the outer `for` again. This effectively creates a non-structured backedge through a label outside the loop body.

That `goto m` is especially important for SSA and loop analysis because it transfers control from inside a loop nest to a label located before the assignment `f = 0` that initializes the controlling induction variable of the outer loop. In CFG terms, this is not a normal loop latch edge but a jump to a predecessor of the loop header/setup region, which can force unusual PHI placement and closed-SSA bookkeeping for values defined inside the loop and used after exiting blocks.

The `a;` statement is a volatile read expression statement. Although it computes no C-level value, it is an observable side effect and therefore cannot be optimized away. This guarantees the outer `for` loop body is not trivially empty and ensures some body content remains even if other statements are simplified.

The condition `if (l) continue;` is always true on entry because `l` is initialized to 1, and the only code that could change it is after this condition. Therefore, on all ordinary executions of the loop body, control hits `continue` before `i = 0;` and before `while (c) l++;`. This means those later statements are dynamically unreachable under normal structured flow. However, optimizers still have to model them correctly until proven unreachable in the transformed CFG.

Because `continue` always fires, `i` normally remains nonzero (`2`, or later possibly reset to `1` by the outer `if (b)` block). That keeps the inner-loop condition `if (i) goto m;` effectively always true whenever the inner loop is reached. Thus the second outer iteration tends to jump to `m`, execute `d = g`, reset `f = 0`, and iterate again. This produces a peculiar control-flow cycle involving the label and loop initializer rather than a canonical loop body/latch arrangement.

The `while (c) l++;` loop is also interesting despite being unreachable on ordinary paths. Since `c` is a global, its value is not generally known at compile time in the abstract program, so GCC must initially preserve a potentially infinite loop that mutates local `l`. Its presence means variable `l` has a live definition spanning continue edges and a possible loop in a dominated but hard-to-reach region, which can complicate SSA name management even if later simplification proves the region dead.

After the `else` block, `if (b) { i = 1; goto k; }` forms another non-structured backedge, this time from the function tail back to the earlier label `k:`. This can make the whole function resemble an outer hand-written loop with a side-entry `else` region containing its own loops and a separate jump target `m`. The combination of gotos and structured loops stresses GCC’s loop discovery and loop-closed SSA verification.

The bug only appears with `-O3 -fno-tree-ch -fno-tree-ccp -fno-tree-fre`. Disabling tree CH, CCP, and FRE is important because those passes would normally simplify or normalize parts of the CFG and dataflow before complete unrolling runs. With them disabled, `cunroll` sees a more awkward CFG/SSA state, preserving the exact combination of constant conditions, labels, unreachable-looking statements, and cross-loop gotos needed to trigger the verifier failure.

The ICE site `check_loop_closed_ssa_def` indicates GCC believes a definition associated with a loop is not properly represented in loop-closed SSA form after or during loop manipulation. Loop-closed SSA requires that values defined in a loop and used outside it flow through appropriate exit PHIs. A jump like `goto m` combined with complete unrolling can create or expose a use/def relation crossing loop boundaries in a way the transformation failed to repair.

The stack trace shows the failure happens during the GIMPLE `cunroll` pass, specifically while `tree_unroll_loops_completely` is operating and then calling `verify_loop_closed_ssa`. That means the source code is valid, but the compiler’s loop transformation likely rewrites or duplicates the small outer `for` loop and leaves behind an inconsistent SSA graph, which is then caught by the verifier rather than producing wrong code silently.

A likely stress pattern in the reproducer is the small constant-bounded outer loop (`f < 2`) combined with a nested loop and a jump to a label preceding the loop initialization. Complete unrolling likes tiny trip-count loops, but unrolling such a loop when its body can transfer control to code that reinitializes the induction variable can break assumptions about natural loop exits and single-entry regions.

Another key feature is that the jump target `m` is textually nested under `if (0)`, so simplification must preserve the label while possibly deleting the guarding conditional. This can produce a CFG where a block survives only as a goto target, and later loop transforms must still treat its statements and PHIs consistently. Such target-only blocks often expose corner cases in CFG and SSA update code.

The reproducer is therefore not about runtime misbehavior of the compiled program but about a compiler internal consistency bug. The code is legal C with gotos into labeled statements inside a compound statement, volatile accesses, and loops. The exercised compiler behavior is: build SSA for unusual goto-based CFG, attempt aggressive `-O3` loop complete unrolling, update SSA/loop metadata, then fail verification because a loop-closed SSA invariant is violated.

From a semantic perspective, the program mostly spins through control flow governed by globals `e` and `b`, with the inner interesting path using `goto m` to assign `d = g` and restart the `f` setup. From a compiler-testing perspective, each construct is chosen to preserve difficult CFG edges: constant-false branch with live label, always-true continue, tiny countable loop, nested loop, volatile access, and non-structured backward gotos. Their interaction is what exercises the faulty GCC transformation path.

This strengthening of the basic ssa form has several advantages: 1) Updating it during unrolling/peeling/versioning is trivial, since we do not need to care about the uses outside of the loop. If CHANGED_BBS is not NULL, we look for uses outside loops only in the basic blocks in this set. USE_FLAGS allows us to specify whether we want virtual, non-virtual or both variables rewritten. At the head of a bb, if there is a predecessor bb that reaches this bb via fallthru, and FOLLOW_FALLTHRU, walks further in the predecessor bb and registers this in DID_FALLTHRU. Otherwise, stops at the head of the bb.

gcc/cfgcleanup.cc.signature: int flow_find_cross_jump (basic_block bb1, basic_block bb2, rtx_insn **f1, rtx_insn **f2, enum replace_direction *dir_p)
gcc/cfgcleanup.cc.summary: Look through the insns at the end of BB1 and BB2 and find the longest sequence that are either equivalent, or allow forward or backward replacement. Store the first insns for that sequence in *F1 and *F2 and return the sequence length. DIR_P indicates the allowed replacement direction on function entry, and the actual replacement direction on function exit. If NULL, only equivalent sequences are allowed. To simplify callers of this function, if the blocks match exactly, store the head of the blocks in *F1 and *F2.

gcc/cfgcleanup.cc.signature: int flow_find_head_matching_sequence (basic_block bb1, basic_block bb2, rtx_insn **f1, rtx_insn **f2, int stop_after)
gcc/cfgcleanup.cc.summary: Like flow_find_cross_jump, except start looking for a matching sequence from the head of the two blocks. Do not include jumps at the end. If STOP_AFTER is nonzero, stop after finding that many matching instructions. If STOP_AFTER is zero, count all INSN_P insns, if it is non-zero, only count active insns.

gcc/cfgcleanup.cc.signature: static bool outgoing_edges_match (int mode, basic_block bb1, basic_block bb2)
gcc/cfgcleanup.cc.summary: Return true iff outgoing edges of BB1 and BB2 match, together with the branch instruction. This means that if we commonize the control flow before end of the basic block, the semantic remains unchanged. We may assume that there exists one edge with a common destination.
Returns true if BB basic block has a preserve label.

gcc/cfgcleanup.cc.signature: static bool try_crossjump_to_edge (int mode, edge e1, edge e2, enum replace_direction dir)
gcc/cfgcleanup.cc.summary: E1 and E2 are edges with the same destination block. Search their predecessors for common code. If found, redirect control flow from (maybe the middle of) E1->SRC to (maybe the middle of) E2->SRC (dir_forward), or the other way around (dir_backward). DIR specifies the allowed replacement direction.

gcc/cfgcleanup.cc.signature: static bool try_crossjump_bb (int mode, basic_block bb)
gcc/cfgcleanup.cc.summary: Search the predecessors of BB for common insn sequences. When found, share code between them by redirecting control flow. Return true if any changes made.
Search the successors of BB for common insn sequences. When found, share code between them by moving it across the basic block boundary. Return true if any changes made.
Return true if BB contains just bb note, or bb note followed by only DEBUG_INSNs.
Return true if BB contains just a return and possibly a USE of the return value. Fill in *RET and *USE with the return and use insns if any found, otherwise NULL. All CLOBBERs are ignored.
Do simple CFG optimizations - basic block merging, simplifying of jump instructions etc. Return nonzero if changes were made.
Delete all unreachable basic blocks.

Delete any jump tables never referenced. We can't delete them at the time of removing tablejump insn as they are referenced by the preceding insns computing the destination, so we delay deleting and garbagecollect them once life information is computed.
Tidy the CFG by deleting unreachable code and whatnot.

reviewed_methods.summary: Given a set of newly created SSA names (NEW_SSA_NAMES) and a set of existing SSA names (OLD_SSA_NAMES), update the SSA form so that: 1- The names in OLD_SSA_NAMES dominated by the definitions of NEW_SSA_NAMES are all re-written to be reached by the appropriate definition from NEW_SSA_NAMES. 2- If needed, new PHI nodes are added to the iterated dominance frontier of the blocks where each of NEW_SSA_NAMES are defined. The mapping between OLD_SSA_NAMES and NEW_SSA_NAMES is setup by calling create_new_def_for to create new defs for names that the caller wants to replace. The caller cretaes the new names to be inserted and the names that need to be replaced by calling create_new_def_for for each old definition to be replaced. Note that the function assumes that the new defining statement has already been inserted in the IL. For instance, given the following code: 1 L0: 2 x_1 = PHI (0, x_5) 3 if (x_1 < 10) 4 if (x_1 > 7) 5 y_2 = 0 6 else 7 y_3 = x_1 + x_7 8 endif 9 x_5 = x_1 + 1 10 goto L0; 11 endif Suppose that we insert new names x_10 and x_11 (lines 4 and 8). 1 L0: 2 x_1 = PHI (0, x_5) 3 if (x_1 < 10) 4 x_10 = ... 5 if (x_1 > 7) 6 y_2 = 0 7 else 8 x_11 = ... 9 y_3 = x_1 + x_7 10 endif

The bug pattern strongly suggests cunroll rewrites CFG/defs but fails to fully rebuild or rewrite SSA/PHIs for awkward cross-loop goto edges; this function is exactly where such repair logic is coordinated.

reviewed_methods.signature: static void rewrite_into_loop_closed_ssa_1 (bitmap changed_bbs, unsigned update_flag, int use_flags)
reviewed_methods.summary: Rewrites the program into a loop closed ssa form -- i.e. inserts extra phi nodes to ensure that no variable is used outside the loop it is defined in. This strengthening of the basic ssa form has several advantages: 1) Updating it during unrolling/peeling/versioning is trivial, since we do not need to care about the uses outside of the loop. The same applies to virtual operands which are also rewritten into loop closed SSA form. Note that virtual operands are always live until function exit. 2) The behavior of all uses of an induction variable is the same. Without this, you need to distinguish the case when the variable is used outside of the loop it is defined in, for example for (i = 0; i < 100; i++) { for (j = 0; j < 100; j++) { k = i + j; use1 (k); } use2 (k); } Looking from the outer loop with the normal SSA form, the first use of k is not well-behaved, while the second one is an induction variable with base 99 and step 1. If CHANGED_BBS is not NULL, we look for uses outside loops only in the basic blocks in this set. USE_FLAGS allows us to specify whether we want virtual, non-virtual or both variables rewritten. UPDATE_FLAG is used in the call to update_ssa. See TODO_update_s
reviewed_methods.reason: Core LCSSA repair routine, so any missed exit PHIs or incomplete renaming could explain check_loop_closed_ssa_def failures. Still somewhat less likely than the unroll/unloop code because the crash occurs during complete unrolling, suggesting the transform likely invalidates SSA incorrectly first.
